meaning: Given the situation, a certain reaction is perfectly understandable: “no wonder ...”, “it's only natural that ...”.
connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／な-adj.・noun + な + のも無理はない

senses.label: No wonder ...
senses.meaning: First give the cause or background, then say a reaction is natural. Like “no wonder ...” or “it's not surprising that ...”. Mostly used to show understanding of someone else's feelings or behavior.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + のも無理はない; the reason often comes first with 「〜のだから」, 「〜なら」 or 「〜では」
examples: He was kept waiting for three hours, so no wonder he's angry.
If it's your first trip abroad, it's natural to be nervous.
With overtime every single day, it's no wonder you're tired.

senses.label: Understandable to think so
senses.meaning: Common as 「〜と思うのも無理はない」 or 「〜されるのも無理はない」. It says someone's judgment or misunderstanding is understandable. It often implies “even though it isn't actually true”.
senses.connection: 〜と思う／〜と考える／passive form + のも無理はない
examples: If you only saw the photo, it's understandable to think it's real.
With an explanation like that, no wonder it gets misunderstood.

senses.label: 無理もない
senses.meaning: 「〜のは無理もない」 means the same. 「無理もない」 can also stand alone, like “No wonder.” or “I don't blame you.”
senses.connection: 〜のは無理もない; 「無理もない」 on its own
examples: It's no wonder she cried.
You're tired, huh. No wonder.

notes: 「〜のも無理はない」 means “no wonder; understandable”, while 「〜のは無理だ」 means “it's impossible to ...”. If you overlook 「は／も」 and 「ない」, you will misread “understandable” as “can't be done”.

Said directly to a superior or customer, 「お怒りになるのも無理はありません」 sounds as if you are judging whether their anger is “reasonable”, which comes across as condescending. To show sympathy, say 「お怒りはごもっともです」 instead.
About yourself it sounds like an excuse: if you are late and say ✕「遅刻したのも無理はない」, people will think you are defending yourself. When you should apologize, just say 「遅れて申し訳ありません」.
After a noun or a な-adjective you need 「な」: ✕「彼が不安のも無理はない」→○「彼が不安なのも無理はない」.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is down after failing an exam, and you show you understand.
daily.example: You worked so hard, so of course you feel down.

daily.title: Talking about the kids
daily.description: Parents mention their child went to bed early.
daily.example: They played outside all day, so no wonder they're sleepy.

daily.title: Chatting about the news
daily.description: Talking with family about a report on rising prices.
daily.example: With prices going up like this, it's no wonder everyone is saving money.

work.title: Explaining a client's complaint to your boss
work.description: A staff member explains why the client complained.
work.example: The delivery was delayed twice, so it's only natural that the client is angry.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: An editorial analyzes residents' reaction to a policy.
work.example: If the explanation is insufficient, it's no wonder residents feel uneasy.

etymology: 「無理」 originally meant “against reason” (理が無い). So 「無理はない」 means “not unreasonable”, hence “it makes sense; no wonder”. In 「のも」, 「の」 turns the clause into a noun and 「も」 means “this too”.

similar.title: 〜のも当然だ・〜のももっともだ
similar.explanation: Both mean “it's only natural that ...”. 「当然だ」 is a calm, assertive judgment and works for good or bad results alike; 「無理はない」 focuses on sympathizing with someone's feelings and reactions, is mostly used for negative situations, and sounds gentler.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: Both can be translated as “no wonder”. 「わけだ」 draws a conclusion from facts and is more logical (「道理で寒いわけだ」); 「のも無理はない」 expresses understanding and sympathy toward a person's feelings or behavior.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 「〜はずだ」 can also express sudden realization (「寒いはずだ、雪が降っている」); it stresses “logically, it should be so”. It does not sympathize with anyone's reaction, and cannot be used to say that someone's feelings are justified.

similar.title: 〜には無理がある
similar.explanation: Same root: both contain 「無理」 (“unreasonable”), but they point in opposite directions. 「〜には無理がある」 says a claim or plan is “far-fetched, unreasonable”; 「のも無理はない」 says a reaction is “perfectly reasonable”.

formation: It is built from 「の」 (which turns the preceding statement into a noun-like unit) + 「も」 + 「無理」 + 「は」 + 「ない」. 「無理」 literally means “no reason”, i.e. unreasonable, so 「無理はない」 is “it is not unreasonable”: a double negative that yields “perfectly reasonable”. 「も」 conveys “in this situation, this reaction too ...”, with a nuance of first acknowledging the background and then showing understanding. Because you are judging whether something is reasonable, the cause is usually stated first (「〜のだから」, 「〜では」), followed by the “no wonder” conclusion.

meaning: Puts forward your opinion or guess softly, in question form: “Isn't it the case that ...?”, “I suspect ...”.
connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／な-adj.・noun + な + のではないだろうか

senses.label: Soft assertion
senses.meaning: The speaker actually has an opinion but uses a question to avoid sounding too sure. More objective and softer than 「〜と思う」. Very common in papers, editorials and speeches.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではないだろうか; nouns and な-adj. take 「な」, e.g. 「必要なのではないだろうか」
examples: Shouldn't this issue have been discussed much earlier?
Isn't young people's drift away from reading linked to the spread of smartphones?

senses.label: Guess
senses.meaning: A guess about something uncertain, like “I suspect ...” or “probably ...”. In speech, 「〜んじゃないだろうか」 is common.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではないだろうか／んじゃないだろうか
examples: Judging by the sky, it might rain from the afternoon.
Hasn't he already gone home?

senses.label: Polite suggestion
senses.meaning: Said to the listener as 「〜のではないでしょうか」, it softly offers a suggestion or opinion. Much more polite than simply saying 「〜です」.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではないでしょうか／んじゃないでしょうか
examples: Wouldn't this plan be more realistic?
Wouldn't it be better to take a little break?

notes: It expresses an affirmative opinion, not a negative one: 「彼が犯人なのではないだろうか」 means “I suspect he is the culprit”, not “he isn't the culprit, is he?”.
Do not drop the final 「か」: 「彼は来るのではないだろう」 means “he probably won't come”, while 「彼は来るのではないだろうか」 means “I wonder if he'll come (I think he will)”. Without 「か」 the meaning is reversed.
To a superior or customer use 「〜のではないでしょうか」. The plain form 「〜のではないだろうか」 belongs to writing or talking to yourself, and the casual 「〜んじゃない？」 sounds too casual and rude to a superior.
After a noun or a な-adjective you need 「な」: ✕「必要のではないだろうか」→○「必要なのではないだろうか」.

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Before a weekend trip, you gently suggest leaving early.
daily.example: The roads will be busy tomorrow, so wouldn't it be better to leave early?

daily.title: Reading an editorial
daily.description: An editorial uses this pattern to state its view softly.
daily.example: Won't this policy actually increase the burden on citizens?

work.title: Raising an objection in a meeting
work.description: Gently voicing concern about your boss's plan.
work.example: Isn't that schedule a little unrealistic?

work.title: Writing a report or paper
work.description: Cautiously stating your judgment in the conclusion.
work.example: From the results above, this method would seem to be effective.

etymology: Made of 「のではない」 (the negative of 「のだ」), plus 「だろう」 (conjecture) and the question particle 「か」. Literally “isn't it probably that ...?”. The negative question ends up expressing a positive guess.

similar.title: 〜のではないか・〜んじゃない
similar.explanation: Same origin and basically the same meaning, but without the conjecture 「だろう」, so it is more direct. 「〜のではないだろうか」 adds a layer of conjecture, making it softer and more like the wording of essays and commentary.

similar.title: 〜ではあるまいか
similar.explanation: Same meaning: both use a negative question to state your guess indirectly. 「ではあるまいか」 uses the literary 「まい」, so it is more bookish and stiff, and is almost never used in conversation.

similar.title: 〜ではなかろうか
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「なかろう」 is the literary form of 「ないだろう」, more archaic, and seen mostly in editorials and academic writing; in everyday conversation use 「〜のではないだろうか」 or 「〜んじゃないかな」.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: Same root: both contain 「のだ」 + 「だろうか」. 「のだろうか」 is a genuine question or self-question (“is it really ...?”) where the speaker has no leaning; 「のではないだろうか」 adds a negation and in fact asserts “I think it is ...”.

formation: It is built from the negative 「のではない」 of 「のだ」 + the conjecture 「だろう」 + the question marker 「か」, literally “isn't it that ...?”. A negative question already expects the answer “yes”, so the whole expression ends up conveying an affirmative guess or claim. Starting from the assertive 「のだ」, each layer (negation, conjecture, question) steps back a little from a flat assertion, which makes the tone very soft and suits stating your own view without sounding dogmatic. 「の」 treats the preceding content as “one fact” to be judged, which is why nouns and な-adjectives need 「な」 first.

meaning: A goes without saying, and B is also true: “not to mention A, B too ...”.
connection: Noun + は言うまでもなく

senses.label: Not to mention A, B too
senses.meaning: First mention A, which is obvious, then add B, which is broader or goes further. The second part often has 「も」, 「まで」 or 「さえ」. Fairly formal.
senses.connection: Noun + は言うまでもなく、noun + も／まで
examples: This restaurant's food is excellent, of course, and so is the service.
He speaks English, needless to say, and also French and Chinese.
This song is popular in Japan, of course, and overseas too.

senses.label: It goes without saying
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, 「〜のは言うまでもない」 means “everyone knows this”, i.e. “it goes without saying that ...”. Common in writing and speeches.
senses.connection: Plain form + の／こと + は言うまでもない／言うまでもありません
examples: It goes without saying that health matters more than anything.
Needless to say, preparing in advance is important.

senses.label: Sentence-initial: needless to say
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, 「言うまでもなく」 works as an adverb: “needless to say”, “as everyone knows”. It introduces a widely accepted fact.
senses.connection: Sentence-initial 「言うまでもなく、〜」
examples: Needless to say, Mt. Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan.
Needless to say, safety comes first.

notes: A must be something that is “obviously true”. In an affirmative sentence put the easy item in A (「ひらがなは言うまでもなく、漢字も書ける」); in a negative sentence put the hard item in A (「漢字は言うまでもなく、ひらがなさえ書けない」). Reverse them and the logic breaks.
Telling a superior or customer 「言うまでもありませんが、締め切りは守ってください」 sounds preachy, as if they lacked common sense. To a superior, say 「念のため申し上げますと」 or 「ご存じのとおり」 instead.
It attaches directly to a noun; a verb phrase must be nominalized first: ✕「時間を守るは言うまでもなく」→○「時間を守ることは言うまでもなく」.

daily.title: Introducing your hometown
daily.description: Recommending your hometown to a friend from abroad.
daily.example: Kyoto has temples, of course, but the Japanese sweets are delicious too.

daily.title: Praising a friend
daily.description: Talking with family about a very capable friend.
daily.example: She's a great cook, needless to say, and her cleaning is perfect too.

work.title: Job posting
work.description: A company states its language requirements.
work.example: Japanese is a given, and English skills are also required.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting the damage caused by an earthquake.
work.example: In this earthquake, not only buildings but also the transport network suffered major damage.

etymology: 「言う」 + 「までもない」. 「〜までもない」 means “there's no need to go as far as ...”, so 「言うまでもない」 is “there's no need to say it”, i.e. “it goes without saying”. The continuative form 「なく」 links to the next clause, giving “A goes without saying, and B too”.

similar.title: 〜はもとより・〜はもちろん
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning. 「はもちろん」 is the most common, fine in speech and writing; 「はもとより」 is more elegant; 「は言うまでもなく」 is more formal than 「はもちろん」 and stresses “needless to say”.

similar.title: 〜は言うに及ばず
similar.explanation: Same root and same meaning: both are built on 「言う」, “there is no need to say”. 「言うに及ばず」 has a literary flavor and is more bookish and solemn, seen mostly in formal writing and speeches.

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: Same root: 「言うまでもなく」 is simply 「言う＋までもなく」. 「までもない」 attaches to many verbs and means “there is no need to ...” (「調べるまでもない」); 「は言うまでもなく」 is a fixed progressive pattern, “A goes without saying, and B too ...”.

similar.title: 〜もさることながら
similar.explanation: Also “A goes without saying, and B too ...”, but 「もさることながら」 grants A while stressing that B is the real point; 「は言うまでもなく」 stresses that A is taken for granted and B is a further extension.

formation: It is built from 「言う」 + 「まで」 (“to the extent of”) + 「も」 + the continuative form 「なく」 of 「ない」, literally “there is not even a need to say it”, i.e. it goes without saying. 「は」 raises A as the topic, and saying A “needn't be mentioned” declares it something everyone takes for granted. 「なく」 is a pausing form, so the sentence is not finished: a further item B must follow, often with 「も」, 「まで」 or 「さえ」 to show the range widening. At the end of a sentence, 「言うまでもない」 simply means “it goes without saying that ...”.

meaning: Puts a topic aside for now to talk about something more important: “setting ... aside”, “leaving ... aside”.
connection: Noun／〜かどうか + はさておき

senses.label: Setting aside
senses.meaning: Shelve the first item for now and focus on the second. The first item isn't unimportant; it's just not being discussed right now.
senses.connection: Noun + はさておき; 〜かどうか／〜か〜か + はさておき
examples: Setting the cost issue aside, let's make a plan first.
Taste aside, it looks really beautiful.
Whether we can do it or not, let's give it a try.

senses.label: Back to the point
senses.meaning: 「冗談はさておき」 and 「それはさておき」 are set phrases that bring the conversation back to the main topic, like “joking aside” or “anyway”.
senses.connection: 冗談／それ／前置き + はさておき
examples: Joking aside, let's get down to business.
Anyway, what's the plan for next week?

notes: Saying ✕「ご意見はさておき」 to a superior or customer means “setting your opinion aside”, which is very rude. 「〜はさておき」 is used only to shelve your own topic, or in set phrases such as 「冗談」 and 「それ」.
「冗談はさておき」 can only be used after you yourself have made a joke; used about what the other person just said, it implies their words were a joke, which hurts.
For a contrast like “A is fine, but B is not”, 「はともかく」 is more natural: 「平日はともかく、週末は混む」 sounds better than 「平日はさておき」. After 「さておき」 you usually get “first, let's ...” or “now to the main point”.
A verb phrase cannot be attached directly; turn it into 「〜かどうか」 or 「〜こと」: ✕「できるはさておき」→○「できるかどうかはさておき」.

daily.title: Getting back to the point after chatting
daily.description: Friends have been chatting for ages, and someone suggests deciding things.
daily.example: Joking aside, let's decide on the trip schedule.

daily.title: Reviewing a restaurant
daily.description: Telling a friend about a place with a great atmosphere.
daily.example: Price aside, it's a place with a really nice atmosphere.

daily.title: Inviting a friend to karaoke
daily.description: Your friend says they're a bad singer, and you encourage them to come.
daily.example: Good or bad, karaoke is fun, right?

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: The chair wants to agree on the overall direction first.
work.example: Leaving the details aside, let's first confirm the overall direction.

work.title: Opening a speech
work.description: After a short greeting, the speaker moves to the main topic.
work.example: Without further ado, let me get straight to the point.

etymology: 「さて」 is an adverb meaning “well, now”, and 「おく（置く）」 means “to put”. 「さておく」 originally meant “to leave something as it is”, and 「さておき」 is its continuative form: “leaving ... aside for now”.

similar.title: 〜はともかく
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning: both say “leaving A aside for now”. 「はともかく」 is more colloquial and often carries a contrast, “A is one thing, but B is the point”; 「はさておき」 stresses shelving the topic and moving to the main subject, and is slightly more formal.

similar.title: 〜は別として
similar.explanation: 「は別として」 excludes A as an exception from the discussion (“that's a separate matter”); 「はさておき」 merely doesn't discuss A for now and may come back to it later.

similar.title: 〜ならいざしらず／〜はいざしらず
similar.explanation: 「はいざしらず」 also means “setting A aside”, but it is more bookish and usually carries a contrast and criticism: “A might be forgivable, but B is not”. 「はさておき」 has no such evaluative tone.

formation: It is built from the adverb 「さて」 + the continuative form 「おき」 of 「置く」. The 「さて」 here is generally believed to be the archaic “as it is, just so” (the same origin as the modern “well then”), so 「さておく」 means “leave it as it is”. With 「は」 making A the topic, saying you “leave A as it is” gives “setting A aside for now”. Because A is “put down”, not “thrown away”, it is not rejected and can be picked up again later, which is why the pattern is often used to change the subject or get back to the point. 「おき」 is a pausing form, followed by what you really want to say; the te-form 「さておいて」 is also possible.

meaning: Leaves the first item aside and puts the focus on the second: “regardless of ...”, “never mind ...”.
connection: Noun／〜かどうか + はともかく(として)

senses.label: Regardless of
senses.meaning: Don't discuss the first item for now; focus on the second. Often implies “A may have problems, but B matters more”.
senses.connection: Noun + はともかく／はともかくとして
examples: Never mind the price, the quality is very good.
Regardless of the result, what matters is that you tried your best to the end.
Design aside, ease of use comes first.

senses.label: A is OK, but B isn't
senses.meaning: The first item is acceptable or understandable, but the second isn't. Gives a contrast like “A is one thing, but B ...”.
senses.connection: Noun A + はともかく、noun B + は〜
examples: Weekdays are fine, but on weekends it's really crowded.
Kids are one thing, but it's a problem when adults don't follow the rules.

senses.label: Whether or not ...
senses.meaning: 「〜かどうかはともかく」 means “leaving aside whether ...”, and the second part gives a different judgment.
senses.connection: 〜かどうか／question word 〜か + はともかく
examples: Whether it's true or not, it's an interesting story.
Whether it succeeds or not, it's worth trying.

notes: 「AはともかくB」 implies a low opinion of A. Saying 「デザインはともかく、機能はいいですね」 about a customer's proposal or a gift from someone implies “the design isn't great”, and can easily offend.
The standalone adverb 「ともかく」 means “anyway, in any case” (「ともかく行ってみよう」) and is not followed by a contrast, so it is not this pattern.
「〜ならともかく」 is hypothetical, “if it were ..., it would be acceptable”: 「子どもならともかく、大人が…」. Replace 「なら」 with 「は」 and it becomes “children aside”, losing the sense that something is forgivable.
A verb phrase cannot be attached directly: ✕「行くはともかく」→○「行くかどうかはともかく」「行くのはともかく」.

daily.title: Commenting on a friend's cooking
daily.description: Your friend cooked for the first time, and it doesn't look great.
daily.example: Never mind the looks, it tastes great!

daily.title: Discussing a travel budget
daily.description: Talking about trip expenses with family.
daily.example: The train fare is fine, but the hotel is way too expensive.

work.title: Reviewing a proposal
work.description: A boss gives feedback on a subordinate's proposal.
work.example: The idea is one thing, but the budget forecast is too optimistic.

work.title: Instructions to staff
work.description: A boss stresses the importance of reporting the process.
work.example: Regardless of the outcome, please report the process properly.

etymology: 「ともかく」 is generally thought to come from 「と」 (that way), 「も」 and 「かく」 (this way), originally meaning “whether this way or that way”. From there came “anyway; leaving aside”. The kanji 「兎も角」 are phonetic borrowings, so it's usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜はさておき
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning. 「はさておき」 stresses shelving the topic and moving to the main point, and is slightly more formal; 「はともかく」 is more colloquial and more often carries the contrast “A aside, B is the point”.

similar.title: 〜ならともかく
similar.explanation: Same root: both contain 「ともかく」. 「ならともかく」 is hypothetical, “if it were A, it would be forgivable (but in fact it's B)”; 「はともかく」 has no hypothesis and simply doesn't discuss A for now.

similar.title: 〜は別として
similar.explanation: 「は別として」 excludes A as an exception (“that's a separate matter”) in a neutral tone; 「はともかく」 simply doesn't discuss A first, and often hints that A has a problem.

similar.title: 〜ならいざしらず／〜はいざしらず
similar.explanation: 「はいざしらず」 is close to 「はともかく」 but more bookish, with stronger criticism (“A is one thing, but B is unacceptable”).

formation: 「ともかく」 is generally thought to be 「と」 (“that way”) + 「も」 + 「かく」 (“this way”), originally “whether that way or this way”, i.e. “regardless”. With 「は」 raising A, saying “A, well, either way is fine” shelves your judgment of A, hence “leaving A aside”. The speaker sets A down on purpose, often because A is problematic or not the point, so a contrast such as “A is okay, but B is the key / B is not acceptable” naturally arises. Adding 「として」 just makes the tone clearer without changing the meaning.

meaning: Just because of one single reason, something bad happened: “simply because ...”, “all because ...”.
connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／な-adj. + な／noun + である + ばかりに

senses.label: Simply because ...
senses.meaning: Just because of this one thing, an unexpected bad result followed. Carries regret, disappointment or frustration. The result is normally negative.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form・nai-form／い-adj.／な-adj. + な／noun + である + ばかりに
examples: I made her angry, all because I said something unnecessary.
I couldn't go to university simply because I had no money.
I've caused you trouble, all because I was careless.

senses.label: Just because I wanted to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜たいばかりに」 means doing something out of a strong desire. The second part is often an unusual effort or sacrifice.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + たい + ばかりに
examples: Just because I wanted to see her, I went to that shop every day.
I studied desperately, just because I wanted my parents to praise me.

notes: The result must be bad (except with 「〜たいばかりに」): ✕「よく勉強したばかりに合格した」→○「よく勉強したおかげで合格した」.
「言ったばかりに」 means “just because I said it”, while 「言ったばかりだ」 means “I have just said it”. One character changes the meaning completely, so check whether a result clause follows.
A noun needs 「である」: 「子どもであるばかりに」 means “just because (he) is a child”; saying 「子どもばかりに」 directly turns it into “only (for) children” and changes the meaning entirely.

About yourself, it is a sincere way of taking responsibility (「私の確認不足だったばかりに、ご迷惑をおかけしました」); said to someone's face, 「あなたが遅れたばかりに」 is a heavy accusation and can damage relations with colleagues and superiors.

daily.title: Regretting looking at your phone
daily.description: Telling a friend about an embarrassing moment.
daily.example: I walked into a utility pole, all because I was looking at my phone while walking.

daily.title: Sharing a regret
daily.description: Complaining to family about missing a trip.
daily.example: I missed my flight, all because I overslept.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes the hero's fate.
daily.example: Simply because he was born into a poor family, he had to give up his dream.

work.title: Apologizing to a client
work.description: The person in charge apologizes for failing to double-check.
work.example: Because we neglected to check, we caused you great inconvenience.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting a system failure caused by a small mistake.
work.example: The entire system went down because of a single person's checking error.

etymology: 「ばかり」 is generally thought to come from the verb 「はかる（量る）」 (to measure). It first meant “extent, about”, then developed the limiting sense “only, just”. With the cause marker 「に」, it came to mean “simply because ...”.

similar.title: 〜せいで
similar.explanation: Both give the cause of a bad result. 「せいで」 simply assigns blame; 「ばかりに」 stresses “just because of this one point”, mostly with regret, and is often used to reflect on yourself.

similar.title: 〜あまり
similar.explanation: Both introduce a negative result. 「あまり」 means a degree that goes too far (「心配するあまり眠れない」); 「ばかりに」 means the cause is just one small point that brought about a big consequence.

similar.title: 〜ばかり（nothing but）
similar.explanation: Same root: 「ばかり」 itself means “only, nothing but”. 「ばかりに」 applies that limiting sense to a cause: “only because ...”.

similar.title: 〜んばかりに／〜んばかりの
similar.explanation: Same root but a different meaning: attached to the stem of the ない-form, it means “as if about to ...” (「泣き出さんばかりに」), describing a manner rather than a cause. The forms look alike and are easily confused.

formation: It is built from 「ばかり」 (“only, merely”) + the case particle 「に」 marking a cause: “only because ...”. Narrowing the cause to “this one thing alone” implies “such a small thing led to such a consequence”, so the pattern naturally carries regret, and the result is mostly bad. In 「〜たいばかりに」, what is narrowed is the wish, “just wanting to ...”, so the result is the effort or cost paid for that wish. 「ばかり」 follows the attributive form of a conjugating word, and a noun is linked with 「である」.

meaning: Something keeps changing in one (usually bad) direction, or someone does nothing but one thing: “just keeps getting ...”, “does nothing but ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ばかりだ

senses.label: Keeps getting ...
senses.meaning: A situation changes in only one direction, with no sign of improvement. Mostly for negative changes. Used with verbs of change such as 「増える」, 「減る」, 「悪くなる」 and 「広がる」.
senses.connection: Change verb in dictionary form + ばかりだ／ばかりです
examples: His condition just keeps getting worse.
Prices have done nothing but rise for the past few years.
The debt just kept growing.

senses.label: Does nothing but ...
senses.meaning: With ordinary action verbs, it means someone just keeps doing one thing and can do nothing else. Often sounds helpless.
senses.connection: Action verb in dictionary form + ばかりだ; often with 「ただ」
examples: No matter what I asked, she just kept crying.
I've caused everyone trouble, and all I can do is apologize.

notes: To mean “more and more ...” you must use the dictionary form: 「人口は減るばかりだ」 means “the population just keeps decreasing”; 「減ったばかりだ」 would mean “the population has just decreased”, which is entirely different.
Mostly used for negative changes. Positive changes generally don't take 「ばかりだ」; something like 「どんどん上手になっている」 is more natural.
「あとは〜ばかりだ」 means “only ... remains; everything is ready” (「あとは出発するばかりだ」), not “more and more”.

daily.title: Complaining about weight
daily.description: Someone who doesn't exercise jokes about their figure.
daily.example: I don't exercise, so my weight just keeps going up.

daily.title: Worrying about family
daily.description: Telling a friend about your grandmother's health.
daily.example: My grandmother's health just keeps getting worse.

work.title: Sales report
work.description: The sales department reports on a new product.
work.example: Sales of the new product have done nothing but fall since its launch.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting on population decline in rural areas.
work.example: Due to the falling birthrate, the population in rural areas keeps shrinking.

etymology: 「ばかり」 originally meant “extent, about”, then came to mean “only, nothing but”. 「〜するばかりだ」 means “there is only this one trend”, hence “keeps moving in one direction”.

similar.title: 〜一方だ
similar.explanation: Both express a one-way change. 「一方だ」 is more objective and can be used for positive or neutral changes; 「ばかりだ」 has a stronger negative coloring and can also mean “just keeps doing something” (「泣くばかりだ」).

similar.title: 〜つつある
similar.explanation: Written style; it objectively describes a change progressing step by step, in a neutral tone. 「ばかりだ」 stresses development in only one direction (mostly bad), with worry or helplessness.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: Same root: both use 「ばかり」 for “only”. 「てばかりいる」 says a person keeps doing the same thing over and over, often with criticism (「遊んでばかりいる」); 「ばかりだ」 focuses on a trend of change or “nothing else can be done”.

similar.title: 〜ばかり（nothing but）
similar.explanation: Same root: 「noun＋ばかり」 means “nothing but ...”. 「dictionary form＋ばかりだ」 applies “only” to actions and changes, meaning “only this one direction”.

formation: It is built from the dictionary form of a verb + the limiting 「ばかり」 (“only”) + 「だ」, literally “there is only the one thing of 「becoming ...」”. After a change verb, it means there is no development other than in that direction, i.e. “more and more ...”; after an ordinary action verb, it means “can only keep doing ...”, with a helpless tone. The dictionary form shows a trend that is not over and still continuing, which is the key; with the ta-form, 「〜たばかりだ」 limits time and becomes “has just ...”.

meaning: The same thing has two opposite sides: “while ..., on the other hand ...”.
connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／な-adj. + な・である／noun + である + 反面

senses.label: Two sides of one thing
senses.meaning: Points out the good and bad sides of the same thing. The two parts are usually contrasting evaluations, like a merit and a drawback. Objective in tone; used in both speech and writing.
senses.connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／な-adj. + な・である／noun + である + 反面
examples: City life is convenient, but on the other hand it's very stressful.
This job pays well, but you get few days off.
The internet makes it easy to get information, but there's also a lot of false information.

senses.label: その反面
senses.meaning: 「その反面」 at the start of a sentence follows on from the previous one: “on the other hand”.
senses.connection: Sentence-initial 「その反面、〜」
examples: He works fast. On the other hand, he makes a lot of mistakes.
The weak yen boosted exporters' profits. On the other hand, import prices went up.

notes: 「反面」 is used only for two sides of the same thing; to compare two different people or things use 「一方で」: ✕「兄は背が高い反面、弟は低い」→○「兄は背が高い一方で、弟は低い」.
The evaluations before and after must be opposite: ✕「便利な反面、値段も安い」→○「便利な反面、値段が高い」.
A noun needs 「である」: ✕「学生反面」→○「学生である反面」; a な-adjective takes 「な」 or 「である」.

In a Japanese sentence the weight falls on the second half. When assessing a customer's proposal, 「斬新な反面、コストがかかります」 puts the emphasis on the drawback; to soften it, put the advantage last: 「コストはかかる反面、斬新です」.

daily.title: Talking about a new place
daily.description: Telling a friend about the apartment you just moved into.
daily.example: It's close to the station, but it's a bit noisy.

daily.title: Talking about having a pet
daily.description: A friend wants a dog, and you share your experience.
daily.example: Dogs are cute, but they're a lot of work to look after.

work.title: Analysis report
work.description: A report objectively weighs the pros and cons of a new system.
work.example: The new system will improve efficiency, but it may increase the burden on frontline staff.

work.title: Self-analysis in a job interview
work.description: A candidate talks about their strengths and weaknesses.
work.example: I'm careful, but on the other hand I tend to take time to make decisions.

etymology: 「反面」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “the opposite side”. Used as a formal noun after a clause, it means “the other, opposite side of this”. 「半面」 originally means “half the surface”, but since it sounds the same it's also used for this pattern.

similar.title: 〜一方（で）
similar.explanation: 「一方で」 can contrast two different subjects, or mean doing another thing at the same time; 「反面」 is used only for two opposite aspects of the same thing, with a stronger contrast.

similar.title: 〜代わりに
similar.explanation: It can also show gains and losses (「給料が高い代わりに残業が多い」), but stresses “in exchange, as compensation”; 「反面」 merely points out the two sides of the same thing objectively, without any idea of exchange.

formation: 「反面」 is a Sino-Japanese word: 「反」 (“opposite”) + 「面」 (“side”), i.e. “the opposite side”. As a formal noun attached to a sentence, it says “this thing that has the stated quality has another side, which is ...”, so the two clauses must be opposite sides of the same subject. Because it is a noun, it follows the attributive form: verbs and い-adjectives directly, な-adjectives with 「な」, nouns with 「である」. 「その反面」 uses 「その」 to refer to the whole preceding matter and is placed at the start of a sentence.

meaning: There's no other way, so this is the only option: “have no choice but to ...”, “can only ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + (より)ほか(は)ない

senses.label: Have no choice but to ...
senses.meaning: You don't want to, but there's nothing else you can do. Sounds resigned. More formal than 「しかない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ほかない／ほかはない／ほかありません
examples: The trains have stopped, so I have no choice but to walk home.
If nobody will help me, I'll just have to do it myself.
The flight was cancelled due to the typhoon, so we had no choice but to give up on the trip.

senses.label: No other way
senses.meaning: Adding 「より」 makes it stronger: “there's no way other than ...”. Also 「〜よりほかに方法がない」 or 「〜よりほかに仕方がない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + よりほかない／よりほかに方法がない
examples: Now that we've come this far, all we can do is see it through to the end.
Right now there's no other way but to follow the doctor's instructions.

senses.label: Can only be called ...
senses.meaning: 「〜というほかない」 means “there's no other way to describe it”: “it can only be called ...”. Used to express a strong impression.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + というほかない
examples: That everyone survived that accident can only be called a miracle.
His behavior can only be called irresponsible.

notes: Do not confuse it with 「〜にほかならない」: 「ほかない」 means “have no choice but to ...” (dictionary form of a verb), while 「にほかならない」 means “is nothing other than ...” (mostly after nouns). ✕「努力の結果にほかない」→○「努力の結果にほかならない」.
It attaches only to the dictionary form of a verb, and generally not to the ない-form: ✕「行かないほかない」. To say “have no choice but to give up”, use 「あきらめるほかない」 or 「行くのをやめるほかない」.
It carries a tone of “no alternative, resignation”. To a customer, 「お客様ご自身でご対応いただくほかありません」 sounds like passing the buck and cold; say 「恐れ入りますが、〜していただけますでしょうか」 instead.
「〜というほかない」 is used for evaluation; 「無責任というほかない」 is harsh criticism, so do not use it about superiors or customers.

daily.title: Missing the last train
daily.description: You stayed out late with friends and missed the last train.
daily.example: I missed the last train, so I'll have to take a taxi home.

daily.title: Something broke
daily.description: Talking with family about a hair dryer that can't be fixed.
daily.example: If it can't be fixed, we'll just have to buy a new one.

work.title: Project delay
work.description: The person in charge explains to the boss that the deadline can't be met.
work.example: Since we're short of staff, we have no choice but to ask for an extension.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A report says rebuilding a disaster area needs long-term support.
work.example: The only way to restore the disaster area is through long-term support.

etymology: 「ほか（外・他）」 means “other, besides”. 「〜ほかない」 means “there's nothing besides this”, hence “this is the only thing to do”. 「より」 is a case particle of limitation, so 「よりほか」 means “other than ...”.

similar.title: 〜しかない（have no choice but to）
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「しかない」 is common in both speech and writing; 「ほかない」 is more bookish and formal, mostly seen in writing and formal speech.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: Both mean “must, cannot help but”. 「ざるを得ない」 stresses being forced by outside circumstances or pressure, against one's wishes; 「ほかない」 focuses on “there is no other option”, with a tone of resignation.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: Same root: both are built on 「ほか」 (“other”), but the meanings differ. 「にほかならない」 = “nothing other than; precisely ...”, used to assert; 「ほかない」 = “no other way, so must ...”.

formation: It is built from 「ほか」 (“outside, other”) + 「ない」, literally “there is nothing other than (doing ...)”. After the dictionary form of a verb, it means “apart from doing this, there is no other way”, i.e. “have no choice but to ...”. Adding 「より」, which marks limitation or comparison, gives 「よりほかない」, which says “other than ...” more explicitly and sounds stronger; inserting 「は」 or 「に」 only adds emphasis. Because all other possibilities are ruled out, it carries a feeling of helplessness and resignation.

meaning: A negative auxiliary expressing negative will (“I will never ...”) or a negative guess (“probably won't ...”). Rather literary.
connection: Godan verb dictionary form／ichidan verb nai-stem + まい (する → するまい・すまい; 来る → 来るまい・来まい)

senses.label: Will never ...
senses.meaning: The speaker's firm determination: “I will never ...”, “never again ...”. The subject is first person. Like 「〜ないつもりだ」 but more literary and stronger. Often with 「二度と」 or 「決して」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + まい; 「二度と〜まい」, 「〜まいと思う／〜まいと決心する」
examples: I'll never go to that awful restaurant again.
I made up my mind never to repeat the same mistake.

senses.label: Probably won't ...
senses.meaning: A negative guess: “probably won't ...”. Like 「〜ないだろう」 but more literary. The subject is usually a third person or a thing.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + まい; 「〜ことはあるまい」, 「〜のではあるまいか」
examples: In this rain, probably nobody else will come.
With his level of ability, he's unlikely to fail.
Nobody would believe a story like that.

senses.label: Try hard not to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜まいとする」 means trying hard to keep something from happening: “try not to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb + まいとする／まいと〜
examples: She looked down so as not to show her tears.
I ran desperately so I wouldn't lose.
I kept quiet about my illness so my parents wouldn't worry.

notes: A godan verb takes the dictionary form, not the ない-form: ✕「行かまい」→○「行くまい」. For ichidan verbs both 「見まい」 and 「見るまい」 are possible; for 「する」 use 「するまい／すまい」.

The same 「まい」 can mean “never will I” or “probably won't”, and the subject tells them apart: 「私は二度と行くまい」 = I will never go again; 「彼はもう来るまい」 = he probably won't come anymore. Misjudge the subject and the meaning is completely different.
「〜のではあるまいか」 and 「〜ではあるまいか」 are actually affirmative guesses (“perhaps it is ...”); do not read them as “surely it isn't ...”.
「まい」 is very literary. Expressing resolve to a superior with 「二度と同じミスはするまい」 sounds like reciting lines; say 「二度と同じミスはいたしません」 instead.

daily.title: Joking after getting drunk
daily.description: After an embarrassing drunken night, you make a vow to a friend the next day.
daily.example: I'm never drinking again.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's determination.
daily.example: He bit his lip, determined not to cry.

work.title: Editorial
work.description: A commentator doubts the effect of the government's measures.
work.example: Measures at this level are unlikely to solve the problem.

work.title: Memorial ceremony speech
work.description: Speaking at a ceremony remembering a disaster.
work.example: We will never forget this tragedy.

etymology: Generally thought to come from the classical negative-conjecture auxiliary 「まじ」, changing 「まじき → まじい → まい」. It is the negative counterpart of the conjecture auxiliary 「う・よう」.

similar.title: 〜だろう
similar.explanation: As negative conjecture, 「まい」 corresponds to 「〜ないだろう」. 「ないだろう」 is used in speech and writing; 「まい」 is more bookish and elegant, and rare in everyday conversation.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: As negative will, 「まい」 corresponds to 「〜ないつもりだ」. 「ないつもりだ」 calmly states an intention; 「まい」 is stronger, with the emotional color of firm resolve.

similar.title: 〜ではあるまいか
similar.explanation: Same root: a fixed pattern made of 「ある＋まい＋か」. Negative conjecture plus a question turns around to mean “probably it is ...”, the opposite of a bare 「まい」.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うか〜まいか
similar.explanation: Same root: it pairs the volitional 「(よ)う」 with its negative 「まい」 to express hesitation, “do it or not” (「行こうか行くまいか迷う」).

formation: 「まい」 is a negative auxiliary, generally thought to derive from the classical 「まじ」, and is exactly the negative counterpart of the volitional/conjectural auxiliaries 「う・よう」. 「う・よう」 expresses will with the first person (「行こう」) and conjecture with others (「雨が降ろう」), so 「まい」 likewise means both “negative will (never ...)” and “negative conjecture (probably not ...)”, distinguished by the person of the subject. The classical 「まじ」 followed the terminal form, so godan verbs take the dictionary form, 「行くまい」; ichidan verbs often take the ない-stem as well as the dictionary form (「見まい」「食べまい」). 「まいとする」 is the negative of 「(よ)うとする」, “try not to ...”.

meaning: Something is simple or obvious, so there's no need to bother doing it: “there's no need to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + までもない／までもなく

senses.label: No need to ...
senses.meaning: The matter is minor or obvious, so there's no need to go to the trouble of doing something. Often with 「わざわざ」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + までもない／までもありません
examples: A cut this small doesn't need a trip to the hospital.
It's close, so there's no need to bother driving me.
That matter is simple, so there's no need to discuss it in the meeting.

senses.label: Without even ...
senses.meaning: 「〜までもなく」 continues into the next clause: “without even needing to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + までもなく、〜
examples: You don't even need to look it up; the answer is obvious.
There's no need to explain; it's just as you all know.

senses.label: 言うまでもない
senses.meaning: 「言うまでもない」 means “needless to say; it goes without saying”. This is the most common set phrase.
senses.connection: 言う + までもない／までもなく
examples: It goes without saying that keeping promises is important.
This goes without saying, but please meet the deadline.

notes: It attaches only to the dictionary form of a verb, not directly to a noun: ✕「確認までもない」→○「確認するまでもない」.
Answering a superior's or customer's question or proposal with 「調べるまでもありません」 or 「聞くまでもないです」 amounts to “need you even ask?”, which sounds arrogant. As a humble lead-in you can say 「ご説明するまでもありませんが」.
「〜ないまでも」 (“even if not ..., at least ...”) looks similar but means something entirely different: 「毎日とは言わないまでも、週に一度は運動したい」.
To reassure someone with “you needn't ...”, 「〜ことはない」 is more natural: 「心配することはないよ」; 「までもない」 stresses that the matter is simple and obvious and lacks that warmth.

daily.title: Turning down help
daily.description: A friend offers to help you carry things.
daily.example: I can carry it myself, so there's no need to help.

daily.title: A minor cold
daily.description: Your family tells you to take medicine.
daily.example: It's just a cold, so there's no need to take medicine.

work.title: Making a call at work
work.description: Coworkers discuss whether to check with the department head.
work.example: For a change this small, there's no need to check with the manager, is there?

work.title: Project review
work.description: Looking back at a failed plan in a meeting.
work.example: Even without looking at the results, it was clear the plan had failed.

etymology: 「まで」 means “up to the point of ...”, 「も」 adds emphasis, and 「ない」 negates. Together: “it doesn't reach the point of needing to ...”, hence “there's no need to ...”.

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are “there is no need to ...”. 「には及ばない」 is politer and more formal, often used to tell the other person “please don't trouble yourself” (「お越しいただくには及びません」).

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: Also “there is no need”, common in speech and mostly used to comfort or advise; 「までもない」 stresses that the matter is simple and obvious and that there is no need to go out of one's way.

similar.title: 〜は言うまでもなく
similar.explanation: Same root: 「言うまでもない」 is the most common fixed combination with 「までもない」, which developed into the progressive pattern “A goes without saying, and B too ...”, with a more fixed usage.

formation: It is built from 「まで」 (“to the extent of”) + 「も」 (emphasis, “even”) + 「ない」, literally “there is not even the need to go as far as doing ...”. 「まで」 itself implies “going out of one's way to some extent”, so what precedes is an action that takes deliberate effort, often paired with 「わざわざ」. Because it speaks of an action not yet done, the dictionary form is used. When 「ない」 becomes the continuative 「なく」 and pauses, it means “without having to ..., (already) ...”.

meaning: Expresses going to extreme, ordinarily unthinkable lengths to achieve a goal: “going so far as to …,” “even doing ….” It often carries the speaker's surprise, incomprehension or criticism.
connection: Noun + までして／までする; verb て-form + まで (+ 〜たくない／〜必要はない etc.)

senses.label: Going as far as (noun)
senses.meaning: With nouns for extreme measures such as 「借金」, 「徹夜」 or 「整形」: “even going so far as to ...”. Often sounds surprised or critical.
senses.connection: Noun + までして／までする
examples: He even went into debt to buy a luxury car.
I even stayed up all night preparing, but the presentation was cancelled.
Do you want to win that badly? (going that far?)

senses.label: Going as far as (verb)
senses.meaning: With the verb te-form. The second part is usually a negative judgment such as 「〜たくない」 or 「〜必要はない」: “it's not worth going that far”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + まで + 〜たくない／〜必要はない／〜とは思わない
examples: I don't want to make money if it means deceiving people.
There's no need to work so hard that you ruin your health.
I don't want to eat it badly enough to wait in line for two hours.

notes: The verb must be in the te-form before 「まで」: 「並んでまで食べたくない」 = I don't want to queue up just to eat; 「並ぶまで」 would mean “until (I) queue up”, with a completely different meaning.

「〜までして」 about someone else's actions often carries a judgment of “why go to such lengths, that's overdoing it”. Saying 「そこまでして〜したんですか」 to a superior or customer sounds like criticism; to express thanks say 「わざわざ〜していただき、ありがとうございます」.
The standalone 「まで」 (「子どもまで笑った」) merely means “even”; this pattern stresses “resorting to extreme means for a goal”, so the preceding item must be a means or a method.

It is easily confused with 「〜てでも」, and swapping them can reverse the attitude: 「借金してでも行きたい」 is “I want to go even if I have to borrow money” (strong will), while 「借金してまで行きたくない」 is “it's not worth borrowing money to go” (a negative evaluation).
The first part must be a costly means that ordinary people wouldn't take; ordinary actions can't be used: ✕「電車に乗ってまで会社に行く」→ ○「熱を押してまで会社に行く」.

daily.title: Talking about a friend
daily.description: You hear a friend skipped school to line up for a game console.
daily.example: I can't believe he'd skip school just to stand in line.

daily.title: Talking about lines
daily.description: A friend invites you to a place with a long line.
daily.example: I don't want to wait two hours just to eat.

daily.title: Talking about dieting
daily.description: A friend is dieting so hard it's hurting her health.
daily.example: There's no need to wreck your health just to lose weight.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: Seeing a report about cosmetic surgery.
daily.example: Some people even go as far as cosmetic surgery to stay young.

work.title: Company policy
work.description: A manager stresses in a meeting that quality comes first.
work.example: We shouldn't cut costs at the expense of quality.

work.title: Talking about work style
work.description: A senior colleague warns a junior about overtime.
work.example: You shouldn't work at the cost of your health.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Criticizing a company for breaking rules to chase profit.
work.example: Pursuing profit to the point of breaking the rules is unacceptable.

etymology: 「まで」 is originally a particle for an endpoint or limit; “reaching the limit of …” extends to “as far as …, even to the extent of ….” 「して」 is the て-form of 「する」, so 「〜までして」 means “going to the point of doing …”; combined with a verb て-form it likewise expresses pushing the means to the extreme for a goal.
formation: 「まで」 is originally a particle for an endpoint or limit (「駅まで」). Attached to the て-form of an action, it treats the act of “doing …” as the point reached: “(for the goal) going all the way to doing …”. This point is seen as the farthest limit, which gives the feel of “even, going so far as,” implying great cost and extreme means. 「Noun + までして」 puts a noun where 「まで」 would take its object and completes the action with 「して」 (the て-form of 「する」): “did even …”. Both say that the means were pushed to the extreme for the goal; the speaker is weighing whether it is worth going that far, so surprise, dissatisfaction or denial naturally follow, and the second half is often an evaluation such as 「〜たくない」「〜必要はない」「〜とは」.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: Both can give an extreme example. 「さえ」 means “even ...”, implying that others go without saying; 「までして」 stresses paying an excessive price for the goal, with surprise or criticism.

similar.title: 〜てでも
similar.explanation: Both mean “not shrinking from the cost”. 「〜てでも」 expresses the speaker's strong will, “I'll do it even if ...” (「借金してでも行く」). 「〜てまで」 is mostly used to judge an extreme means already taken or possible, and the second half is often negative or surprised (「借金してまで行きたくない」).

meaning: Doing something without caring about things you normally should: “regardless of ...”, “without caring about ...”.
connection: Noun／verb plain form + の + もかまわず

senses.label: Regardless of ...
senses.meaning: Not caring at all about things people usually pay attention to (others' eyes, the place, danger, etc.) and doing it anyway. Often shows the speaker's surprise or criticism.
senses.connection: Noun + もかまわず; verb plain form + の + もかまわず
examples: He burst out crying loudly, not caring who was watching.
The children ran around in the rain, not caring that their clothes got wet.
Ignoring the doctor's warnings, my father keeps smoking.

senses.label: Set phrases
senses.meaning: 「所かまわず」 (anywhere at all), 「なりふりかまわず」 (without caring how one looks) and 「誰かれかまわず」 (to anyone at all) are common idioms. They don't take 「も」.
senses.connection: 所／なりふり／誰かれ + かまわず
examples: He talks loudly on the phone wherever he is.
I worked without caring how I looked and paid off my debt.

notes: Do not confuse it with 「〜てもかまわない」 (“it's fine even if ...”, expressing permission): 「濡れるのもかまわず走った」 = ran without caring about getting wet; 「濡れてもかまわない」 = it's okay to get wet.
With a verb, nominalize with 「の」 first: ✕「濡れるもかまわず」→○「濡れるのもかまわず」.

The subject is mostly someone else, and the speaker is critical or surprised. Saying 「人目もかまわず」 about a superior or customer implies they disregard appearances, so never say it in front of them or to them.

The related 「どうぞお構いなく」 is a polite phrase meaning “please don't go to any trouble” when visiting, and the host's 「何のお構いもできませんで」 means “I'm sorry I couldn't entertain you properly”; neither means “I don't care”.

etymology: 「かまう（構う）」 means “to mind, to look after”. 「かまわず」 is the literary continuative negative form (ず-form), so 「〜もかまわず」 means “not even minding ...”.

similar.title: 〜を顧みず／〜も顧みず
similar.explanation: Very close in meaning: both are “without regard to ...”. 「顧みず」 is more bookish, mostly for disregarding danger, family, or one's own safety, and often positive (「危険も顧みず救助した」); 「もかまわず」 is mostly critical, often about others' eyes or the occasion.

similar.title: 〜をよそに
similar.explanation: Written style, indicating ignoring other people's worries, expectations, or opposition; 「もかまわず」 is more common, and its objects are mostly others' eyes, the occasion, or danger.

similar.title: 〜をものともせず
similar.explanation: Also “not treating ... as a big deal”, but its objects are difficulties or obstacles, with a tone of praise (「嵐をものともせず」); 「もかまわず」 is mostly critical.

similar.title: 〜てもかまわない
similar.explanation: Same root: both come from 「構う」 (“to mind”). 「てもかまわない」 gives permission, “it's fine even if ...”; 「もかまわず」 means “(doing something) without caring at all”. The meanings differ and they cannot be swapped.

formation: It is built from 「も」 (“even”) + the negative 「かまわ＋ず」 of 「構う」 (“to mind, to care about”). 「ず」 is the continuative form of the classical negative auxiliary and acts as a pause, equivalent to 「かまわないで」. As a whole: “not caring even about A, (did the following)”. 「も」 implies that A is something one ought to have cared about (others' eyes, the occasion, danger), so the sentence naturally conveys the speaker's surprise or criticism. A noun is required before it; a verb must first be nominalized with 「の」.

meaning: Not exactly the same, but in practice no different: “as good as ...”, “practically ...”.

senses.label: Practically the same as
senses.meaning: It's different in form, but in reality almost the same as the first item. A subjective judgment by the speaker, often exaggerated.
senses.connection: Noun + も同然だ／も同然の + noun
examples: I see him every day, so he's practically family.
I've only used this computer once, so it's as good as new.

senses.label: As good as done
senses.meaning: With the verb ta-form: it hasn't fully happened yet, but the result is basically settled.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + も同然だ
examples: With a lead this big, we've as good as won.
The contract has been signed, so it's as good as decided.

senses.label: ただ同然
senses.meaning: In phrases like 「ただ同然」 (“practically free”), the noun attaches directly to 「同然」 and 「も」 is dropped.
senses.connection: ただ + 同然（の／で）
examples: I bought these clothes at a sale for next to nothing.
I was given some old furniture practically for free.

notes: 「同然（どうぜん）」 is not 「当然（とうぜん）」: 「勝ったも同然」 = as good as won; ✕「勝ったも当然」 makes no sense.
A verb must be in the ta-form: ✕「勝つも同然」→○「勝ったも同然」; a noun takes 「も同然」 directly.
Applied to people it carries weight: 「家族も同然だ」 is an affectionate remark, but 「泥棒も同然だ」 and 「素人も同然だ」 are harsh put-downs and must never be said of a superior or customer.

「決まったも同然」 means it has not actually been decided yet; if you report 「契約は決まったも同然です」 to a superior and the deal falls through, it will be seen as a false report, so state the real status when reporting.

etymology: 「同然」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “the same”. 「も」 means “even if you call it ...”, so 「〜も同然」 is “you might as well call it ...”.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 「ようだ」 expresses a comparison or conjecture, merely “it seems like ...”; 「も同然」 stresses that there is no difference in substance, “it's no exaggeration to call it ...”, a stronger and more exaggerated judgment.

similar.title: 〜と同じ
similar.explanation: Same root: both use 「同」. 「と同じ」 objectively says two things are the same; 「も同然」 is the speaker's subjective view that “though not exactly so, it amounts to the same”, often exaggerated.

similar.title: 〜かのようだ
similar.explanation: 「かのようだ」 means “as if ...”, on the premise that it is not actually so, and is descriptive; 「も同然」 asserts that there is practically no difference.

formation: It is built from 「も」 + the Sino-Japanese word 「同然」 (「同」 = “same”, 「然」 = “state”) + 「だ」. Here 「も」 has a concessive sense, “even if you call it A, ...”, and 「同然」 is “the same”; together: “even calling it A would be the same”, i.e. “in substance it equals A”. Because of the concessive 「も」, it implies “strictly speaking it isn't A”, so it is the speaker's subjective judgment and often an exaggeration. After a verb the ta-form is used, meaning “the result already amounts to completion”.
